why:
Section 8.1.3 states that hydrogen has three isotopes, with mass numbers 1, 2 and 3, all containing one proton and one electron and differing only in the number of neutrons. Of these three, the chapter's "Do you know ?" box singles out exactly one as unstable: tritium, \(^{3}_{1}\mathrm{H}\), described as a radioactive nuclide with a half-life period of 12.4 years which emits low-energy \(\beta\) particles. A radioactive nuclide is by definition one whose nucleus decays, i.e. an unstable isotope, so the isotope of mass number 3 is the one asked for.

Why the others fail. Protium (mass number 1) is ordinary hydrogen, the overwhelmingly dominant natural form, and the chapter attributes no radioactivity to it. Deuterium (mass number 2) is the heavy-hydrogen isotope used to make heavy water \((\mathrm{D_2O})\); the chapter likewise records no decay for it, and only tritium is flagged in the radioactivity note. The remaining choice, mass number 4, is not an isotope of hydrogen at all so far as this chapter is concerned — section 8.1.3 states plainly that hydrogen has three isotopes, and neither the text nor table 8.1 recognises a fourth — so it cannot be the intended answer even though a nuclide of that mass number is known to nuclear physics as an extremely short-lived species outside the scope of this book.

Hence the unstable isotope of hydrogen is tritium, H-3.

The question asks which member of the set does not share the property common to the rest, so the test is group membership. Section 8.2.1 states that group 2 of the periodic table consists of beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium, collectively called the alkaline earth metals. Three of the four choices — radium, strontium and beryllium — appear in that list, so all three are alkaline earth metals with the outer electronic configuration \(ns^2\) given in section 8.2.2, and each of them forms a dipositive \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion.

Rubidium is not in that list. It belongs to group 1, the alkali metals, whose general outer electronic configuration section 8.2.2 gives as \(ns^1\) and which form monopositive \(\mathrm{M^{\oplus}}\) ions. It is therefore the one element of the four that differs from the other three in group, in outer configuration and in the charge of its common ion.

Beryllium is a tempting choice because it is the anomalous member of group 2 — the chapter notes that it alone does not react with water and that its compounds are covalent — but it is still an alkaline earth metal, so it shares group membership with radium and strontium and is not the odd one. Radium being radioactive is likewise a property of that individual element and not a difference of group. The odd one out is rubidium.

A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor, so the chloride wanted here is the one whose metal centre is electron deficient and has a vacant orbital able to accept a lone pair. Table 8.8 of this chapter, which sets out the diagonal relationship between Be and Al, answers the question directly: against the criterion "Whether Lewis acid" it records that \(\mathrm{BeCl_2}\) is a strong Lewis acid, exactly as \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) is, and in the same table it records that the group 2 chlorides in general are "Not Lewis acid". Beryllium chloride is the exception because, as the same table shows, its bonding is covalent and it exists as a chain structure with chlorine bridges — bridging being precisely the consequence of the electron deficiency at beryllium, which carries only four electrons around it in the monomer.

Why the others fail. Barium chloride is the chloride of a large, strongly electropositive group 2 metal; table 8.8's "Not Lewis acid" entry for group 2 covers it, its bonding being ionic rather than covalent. Potassium chloride is an ionic group 1 halide of the kind described in section 8.2.4, formed by complete transfer of the single \(ns^1\) electron, with \(\mathrm{K^{\oplus}}\) already at an inert-gas configuration and no tendency to accept a further electron pair. Lithium chloride is the closest of the three to an exception, since Problem 8.6 of this chapter shows that the small, highly charge-dense \(\mathrm{Li^{\oplus}}\) ion polarises the chloride ion and gives LiCl partial covalent character; but partial covalent character is not electron deficiency, and the chapter names only \(\mathrm{BeCl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) as Lewis acids. The Lewis acid among the four is beryllium chloride.

"Crystalline" sodium carbonate is the hydrated salt: section 8.3.1 titles the compound washing soda, \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \cdot 10H_2O}\), and describes it as a white crystalline solid. Its properties paragraph then states what heating does to it — on heating, the decahydrate loses water molecules to form the monohydrate, and on heating above 373 K the monohydrate further loses water and changes into the white anhydrous powder called soda-ash. The chapter prints both steps as equations:

\(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \cdot 10H_2O(s)} \xrightarrow{373\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \cdot H_2O(s)} + 9\mathrm{H_2O(g)}\)

\(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \cdot H_2O(s)} \xrightarrow{>\,373\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{Na_2CO_3(s)} + \mathrm{H_2O(g)}\)

So what is lost on heating is water of crystallisation, and the residue is the anhydrous carbonate.

Why the others fail. Carbon dioxide is not released: in both printed equations the only gaseous product is water vapour, and the carbonate ion survives intact. It is sodium bicarbonate, not sodium carbonate, that gives off carbon dioxide on heating — the second stage of the Solvay process in this same section is \(2\,\mathrm{NaHCO_3(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{Na_2CO_3(s)} + \mathrm{H_2O(g)} + \mathrm{CO_2(g)}\), which produces sodium carbonate rather than consuming it. Decomposition into sodium bicarbonate is therefore the Solvay reaction run backwards and does not occur; heating drives that reaction forwards. A colour change is excluded because both the starting decahydrate and the soda-ash product are described as white. Heating crystalline sodium carbonate makes it lose its water of crystallisation.
